stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researchers' conclusion?
stimulus: In a Norwegian fjord, common periwinkles from a sheltered inner site have shells about 30 percent thicker than periwinkles from an outer site near the fjord's mouth. The water at the inner site averages about 3°C warmer, and shore crabs, which crush periwinkles, are far more abundant there. In many mollusks, warmer water speeds shell deposition, so the difference could simply be a by-product of temperature. Marine biologist Sigrun Aasen and colleagues, however, concluded that the periwinkles thicken their shells in response to chemical cues released by crabs, not because of the warmer water.
choices: Surveys over several years found that inner-site periwinkles consistently had thicker shells and lived among more crabs than outer-site periwinkles did.
Outer-site periwinkles kept in crab-free tanks grew thicker shells when their water was warmed to the inner site's temperature than when it was not.
Outer-site periwinkles kept in tanks at the outer site's temperature grew thicker shells when given water that had held crabs than when given crab-free water.
Periwinkles taken from the outer site and caged at the inner site grew shells as thick as those of inner-site periwinkles within a single year.
explanation: The conclusion has two parts: crab cues cause the thickening, and warmth does not. To support both, a finding has to vary the crab cue while holding temperature fixed. Choice C does exactly that. Outer-site snails were kept at the colder outer-site temperature, and the only difference between the two groups was whether their water had held crabs. The cue group still grew thicker shells, so the cue alone produced the effect without any extra warmth.

A.why: This just restates the observation the passage starts with: thick shells and many crabs at the inner site. The researchers' explanation and the temperature explanation both predict this pattern, so it can't help you choose between them. You picked a finding that repeats the result instead of isolating its cause.

B.why: Here warmth alone, with no crabs, thickened the shells. That supports the alternative the researchers rejected, so it weakens their conclusion. You probably saw a controlled tank experiment with thicker shells and missed which variable was changed.

D.why: This is the trap for students who already know they need an experiment. Moving the snails to the inner site exposes them to more crabs and to warmer water at the same time. Their shells would thicken under either explanation, so the result can't show that crabs rather than temperature are responsible. You read support for one cause into a result that two causes explain equally well.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researchers' hypothesis?
stimulus: On dairy farms in western Ireland, barn swallow pairs nesting in barns that house cattle fledge more chicks per brood than pairs nesting in barns left empty. Cattle barns differ from empty ones in two relevant ways. Dung and animals attract large numbers of flies, a staple of nestling diets, and the cattle's body heat keeps the air several degrees warmer. Ornithologist Teodor Lindqvist and colleagues hypothesize that the swallows' advantage in cattle barns comes from the flies, which allow parents to bring food to nestlings more often, rather than from the added warmth.
choices: When fly traps cut fly numbers in cattle barns but left air temperature unchanged, both parents' feeding rates and fledging success fell toward empty-barn levels.
Within cattle barns, pairs that made more feeding trips per hour went on to fledge more chicks than did pairs in those barns that made fewer trips.
Throughout the nesting season, cattle barns held both far more flies and noticeably warmer air than did the empty barns on the same farms.
Parents in cattle barns and in empty barns made feeding trips at similar rates, but chicks in cattle barns lost less weight on cold nights.
explanation: Break the hypothesis into a chain and a rival. The chain runs from flies to more frequent feeding to more fledglings. The rival, warmth, is said not to be the cause. Choice A removes the first link (flies) while holding the rival (temperature) fixed. The middle link (feeding rate) and the outcome (fledging success) then both fall. That one finding supports every link in the chain and rules out warmth as the explanation.

B.why: This is the trap for students who see that feeding rate is the key link. It shows only that more feeding goes with more fledglings, and only inside cattle barns. It says nothing about whether flies cause the extra feeding. Warmer air could also free parents to make more trips. You confirmed one link of the chain and treated it as support for the whole hypothesis.

C.why: Both proposed causes are higher in cattle barns, which the passage already says. A finding that holds equally for both explanations can't separate them. You chose a statement that fits the hypothesis instead of one that singles out flies as the cause.

D.why: Similar feeding rates break the middle link the researchers depend on. Chicks staying heavier on cold nights points to warmth instead. This finding weakens the hypothesis. You may have noticed that cattle-barn chicks did better and missed which cause that benefit points to.
